newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern Africa yet to deal with impact of AIDS.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa yet to deal with impact of AIDS.

text.p: AIDS has swept through Africa's southern economic bloc but its full impact has yet to be realised, an economics professor said on Friday.

Professor Alan Whiteside, of the Natal University economics research department, said in an interview the high incidence of AIDS in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region would strain the economies of its 12 member states.

The more sophisticated industrial economies of South Africa, emerging as one of the most pivotal in the region following the lifting of international sanctions against white rule, Zimbabwe and Botswana were particularly at risk, he said.
"SADC economies are poised for growth with the ending of apartheid and the peace dividend. However, the imminent AIDS epidemic will at the very least slow this down.
"The danger is the more sophisticated and developed the economy the greater its vulnerability," Whiteside said.
"Countries which depend on life insurance, pension funds and other formal saving mechanisms may see a decline in money available for investment.
"Illness and death of skilled and experienced staff, who are in short supply, may further cripple operations of the formal sector economies," he said.

United Nations figures show there are 14 million people with the Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) in sub-Saharan Africa. The next worst affected region is south and southeast Asia with 5.2 million cases out of 22.6 million cases worldwide.
"There can be no doubt that the AIDS epidemic is one of the major challenges facing SADC countries," said Whiteside.

But he cautioned: "There is a serious problem in trying to understand the impact of AIDS on economies in the region because the disease is still so new. It will take between 50 and 75 years for the full impact of the epidemic to be felt."
Whiteside said preventative measures had largely failed in southern Africa, adding one reason was that donor nations had taken control of projects which governments should be handling.
"The problem with donor support is that the government loses ownership of the problem, and then does not take responsibility for it," he told Reuters.

The SADC which groups Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe represents 40 percent of Africa's population -- and 80 percent of the continent's GDP.
